title: Dan Campbell Denies Firing Kelvin Sheppard Rumors, Says He's Not Discussing It – NBC Sports
body:
The Detroit Lions’ defense has become the focal point of a growing crisis, prompting head coach Dan Campbell to address rumors of a possible staff shake‑up after the team’s third straight loss, this one a 32‑26 defeat at the hands of the Carolina Panthers on Sunday night. While the Lions’ offense managed to move the ball efficiently, the unit on the other side of the ball surrendered 445 total yards, a statistic that has intensified calls from fans and analysts alike for a change in defensive leadership. Campbell, however, stopped short of confirming any firings, specifically denying that linebackers coach Kelvin Sheppard is on the chopping block, but he warned that “something has to change” if Detroit hopes to stay competitive in the NFC North.

The Lions entered the 2026 campaign with lofty expectations after a modestly successful 2025 season that saw the team finish 9‑8 and narrowly miss the playoffs. Yet, the first three weeks have exposed glaring deficiencies in a defense that struggled to stop both the run and the pass. In Week 1 against the Chicago Bears, Detroit allowed 381 yards and failed to generate a single sack, while Week 2 versus the Minnesota Vikings saw the Lions concede 398 yards and three turnovers forced by the opposition. The Panthers’ 32‑26 victory continued the trend, as Detroit’s secondary gave up 28 completions for 312 yards, and the front seven could not contain Carolina’s balanced attack, which featured 133 rushing yards and 312 through the air.

Analysts have pointed to a lack of identity on the defensive side of the ball as a core issue. The Lions’ scheme appears to vacillate between aggressive blitz packages and conservative zone coverages, leaving players uncertain about assignments. Defensive end Aidan Hutchinson, who was expected to be a dominant pass rusher, has recorded only two sacks in the first three games, while rookie safety Jalen Carter has been repeatedly beaten deep, suggesting communication breakdowns in the secondary. Moreover, the unit’s inability to generate pressure has left quarterback Jared Goff exposed, contributing to a modest 2‑3 turnover ratio that has cost the team in close contests.

Campbell’s comments on the sidelines have been measured but unmistakably urgent. “We’re not looking at firing anyone at this moment,” he told reporters after the Panthers game, “but we are evaluating every piece of the puzzle. Our goal is to get better each week, and that starts with accountability.” The head coach’s refusal to name Sheppard specifically appears to be a strategic move to keep the coaching staff focused while the front office evaluates performance metrics. Sources close to the organization indicate that General Manager Brad Holmes has already begun reviewing the defensive coaching roster, with a particular emphasis on the pass‑rush coordinator and secondary coaches, to determine whether a change in philosophy or personnel is warranted.

The Lions’ front office faces a delicate balancing act. On one hand, the team’s salary cap situation limits the ability to make marquee free‑agent signings in the defensive backfield or front line. On the other, the organization has a pool of young talent on rookie contracts who could be thrust into larger roles if the coaching staff decides to shift schemes. Defensive coordinator Aaron Glenn, who took over after the 2024 season, has hinted at possible adjustments to a more aggressive 4‑3 alignment that could better leverage Hutchinson’s pass‑rush abilities, but such a transition would require a period of adaptation that the Lions can ill‑afford in a tightly contested division.

Looking ahead, Detroit’s next two games against the Green Bay Packers and the Chicago Bears present crucial opportunities to gauge whether the defensive unit can respond to the mounting pressure. If the Lions can tighten coverage, increase quarterback pressure, and reduce big plays, Campbell may find the justification to retain his current staff and focus on development. Conversely, continued lapses could accelerate the decision‑making process, potentially resulting in mid‑season coaching changes that have become increasingly common in the NFL. For now, the Lions’ fans remain hopeful that the “hard‑nosed” identity promised by Campbell will materialize on the field, but the clock is ticking, and the margin for error continues to shrink.
